newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco gets more bad news as settlement talks proceed.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco gets more bad news as settlement talks proceed.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

While cigarette makers struggle to find a solution to mounting civil litigation, the industry also faces a Justice Department criminal probe and now Philip Morris Cos. is the target of a Federal Trade Commission investigation.

The industry was hit with more bad news as it held talks with a core group of attorneys general Thursday aimed at resolving state suits seeking to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers along with hundreds of individual and class action cases brought by smokers and their families.
Federal prosecutors are not involved in the talks and if a settlement is reached it would not stop the filing of potential criminal charges against the industry or its present or current officials.

One Capitol Hill source said he believed the threat of the federal probes would help push settlement talks forward as the industry would want to resolve the civil liability question before possibly being hit with criminal charges. However, attorneys general who have sued the industry said that progress remains slow.
At issue is whether the negotiators can develop a plan that would give the tobacco industry some certainty about how much it would have to pay in damages while preserving individuals' right to sue.

Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal, who heads a committee considering the civil liability question, said Thursday he still believes that the chance an accord can be reached is no more than "50-50."
"All of us are still hopeful though," he said.
On Thursday, Justice Department officials said that more FBI agents have been added to work on its wide-ranging criminal investigation into the tobacco industry.

The Justice Department is investigating allegations that the industry and its top executives withheld information and lied to Congress and federal agencies about the effects of nicotine and other health risks of smoking.
The officials said the agents had been added several weeks ago, and that the investigation is moving forward.
The probe received a boost in March when the Liggett Group, the smallest of the cigarette makers, agreed to settle the 22 Medicaid suits that had been filed at that time.
Under the pact, Liggett, which is owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group, agreed to turn over internal tobacco documents and admitted that nicotine is addictive.
The company has just begun to add warning labels about nicotine to its cigarettes. However, other manufacturers deny that nicotine is addictive.
Justice Department officials said that the additional FBI agents had been needed to help carry out the investigation, including reviewing newly available documents.
"The case involves millions of pages of documents," one official said. The department is reviewing internal documents from Liggett.

On Wednesday Philip Morris said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that the FTC had launched an investigation in to whether it unfairly restricts the distribution of competing brands.

These developments occur while the number of civil lawsuits continues to rise. At least 29 attorneys general have sued the industry including South Carolina, the biggest tobacco producing state, filing earlier this week.
The tobacco industry also faces more than 300 individual and class action lawsuits filed by smokers, their families, and people claiming to be injured from second-hand smoke.
The attorneys general along with plaintiffs lawyers and members of the health community began negotiating with the tobacco industry last month in an attempt to resolve the mounting civil litigation.
They held a large meeting with the tobacco industry last week in Dallas. The parties had originally planned for another big session this week, but only the core group of negotiators is meeting.
Philip Morris' stock rose 25 cents to $42.75, while Brooke gained 12.5 cents to $4.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
